content: The slug is a unit of mass used in the English system. It is defined as the amount of mass that experiences an acceleration of 1 foot per second squared (ft/s²) when subjected to a force of one pound-force (lbf). In terms of metric units, one slug is equivalent to approximately 14.5939 kilograms. Mathematically, 1 slug is equal to ( frac{text{lbf} cdot text{s}^2}{text{ft}} ). The slug is part of a subset of coherent units known as the gravitational foot-pound-second (FPS) system. This system is one of several specialized systems of mechanical units that were developed during the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The term slug was first introduced in 1902 by Arthur Mason Worthington (1852–1916) in his work Dynamics of Rotation. However, the unit did not gain widespread usage until several decades later. A textbook from 1928 noted that no specific name had yet been assigned to the unit of mass in this system. The text explained that, in practice, the mass ( m ) was often expressed as the ratio of a convenient force-acceleration pair (weight divided by gravitational acceleration, ( w/g )), and mass was measured in pounds squared (lbs²). This suggests that the need for a distinct name for the unit of mass was not initially considered essential. In earlier literature, the slug was sometimes referred to by another name: the geepound. Additionally, there are variations of the slug that are based on different length units. For example, the slinch (a portmanteau of slug-inch) is the inch-based version of the slug. One slinch is defined as ( 1 , text{lbf} cdot text{s}^2 / text{in} ), which is equivalent to 12 slugs. Another inch-based version of the slug is the blob (abbreviated as bl), which is also defined as ( 1 , text{lbf} cdot text{s}^2 / text{in} ).
